title: The Voynich Manuscript: 600 Years and No One Can Read It
description:
The Voynich manuscript is a 15th-century book of strange plants, star charts and bathing women, written in a script that no codebreaker, linguist or computer has ever read. Here is the full story of the world's most mysterious manuscript.

We follow the book from its carbon-dated calfskin pages (1404 to 1438), through the Prague alchemist Georg Baresch, Athanasius Kircher, the story of Emperor Rudolf's 600 ducats, the Jesuits of Rome and the book dealer Wilfrid Voynich, to Yale's Beinecke Library, where it is MS 408. Then the evidence: the statistics, the scribes, the World War codebreakers who failed, and the main theories, from cipher and lost language to hoax.

Cipher, lost language, or beautiful nonsense: what do you think the Voynich manuscript really is? Tell me in the comments.
look: early 15th-century Europe and later archives: worn calfskin vellum codex, iron gall ink, crude azurite blue and ochre paint, candlelit studies, dusty Jesuit libraries, 1940s codebreaking offices

short.caption:
A 600-year-old book, 240 pages, and not one word anyone can read.
Codebreakers from both world wars tried and failed.
Cipher, lost language or hoax: what do you think it is?
short.narration: What would you do with 240 pages you could never read, not even one word? This book is called the Voynich manuscript. Its calfskin pages were carbon-dated to between 1404 and 1438. Every page carries writing, in a script no one has ever identified. There are plants no one can name, and wheels of stars. There are small women bathing in pools joined by pipes. In 1639, a Prague alchemist sent a sample to a scholar in Rome, asking for help. He called the book a Sphinx. A later letter says he gave up hope only with his life. In 1912, a book dealer named Wilfrid Voynich bought it, and it took his name. Codebreakers from both world wars studied it. Every one of them failed to read it. Its word patterns look like those of a real human language. But its letters repeat in ways no known language does. Some say it hides a cipher, some a lost language. Others call it a careful hoax that means nothing. Today it sits at Yale, and every page is online. Around 38,000 words, still waiting for a reader. So is there a message in those pages, or nothing at all? Tell me what you think happened. The full case file is on StoryVaultFiles.
